Top bank resets Tesla stock target, yet standalone value is alarming
Moz Farooque, Robert Davey

HSBC

Wall Street ended a bruising week on Friday, November 20, as the deepening AI stock rout pushed the S&P 500 into correction territory and wiped out the Nasdaq's gains for the entire year, as reported by Yahoo Finance.

Caught squarely in the crosshairs was Tesla (TSLA), which took a big hit alongside Silicon Valley's biggest names as nervous investors dumped several high-multiple growth stocks. Interestingly, the stock's slide happened on the very same day one of Wall Street's biggest Tesla skeptics finally blinked. 

In a November 20 note, HSBC analyst Michael Tyndall upgraded the stock from Reduce to Hold and more than doubled his 12-month price target. Yet beneath that headline reversal, the math tells a far more unsettling story.

Inside HSBC's $359 reset, and the alarming $212 standalone floor underneath

Tyndall's note switched up how HSBC values the $1.37 trillion automaker. 

More Tesla:

Tesla stock sellers should pump their brakes, 5-star analyst says

Bank of America resets Tesla forecast as Robotaxi miles double

Tesla wants to sell a car with no steering wheel this year

Previously, the bank anchored its bearish stance on Tesla's core operations, noting that third quarter sales hit $28.05 billion ($20.56 billion from autos) and free cash flow reached $1.53 billion, even as U.S. electric vehicle demand cooled after the $7,500 federal tax credit expired and China's market share narrowed.

That said, in the note HSBC nudged its standalone discounted cash flow valuation up only slightly, from $193 to $212 per share. Against Tesla's November 19 closing price of $374.41, that implied 43.4% downside; even after Friday's drop to $345.82, it still represents a 38.7% haircut.

To arrive at his $359, Tyndall split his valuation 50/50, layering that $212 standalone figure with a hypothetical SpaceX takeover (SPCX) at $507 per share, which assumes a hefty 33% acquisition premium over Tesla's trailing 30-day average price.

Ironically, Friday's rout pushed Tesla slightly behind HSBC's new target (+3.8% upside), even though $359 suggested downside at the time. 

What Elon Musk really wants from a SpaceX–Tesla merger

Deal talk is far from being simply idle speculation. 

On October 20, Elon Musk confirmed that both companies had formed special committees of independent directors to explore a combination, with Bloomberg reporting that an announcement could arrive as early as December or early 2027.

title: J.P. Morgan Says Tesla’s Robotaxi Fleet Could Match Waymo’s Miles by Late 2027 With 18,000 Cars. The Number That Matters Is How Much Each Car Earns.
detail:
J.P. Morgan Says Tesla’s Robotaxi Fleet Could Match Waymo’s Miles by Late 2027 With 18,000 Cars. The Number That Matters Is How Much Each Car Earns.
Lee Samaha, The Motley Fool
Sun, November 22, 2026 at 6:32 AM MST 4 min read
TSLA
GOOGN
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

J.P. Morgan analyst Rajat Gupta believes that Tesla's (NASDAQ:TSLA) robotaxi fleet could match Alphabet's (NASDAQ:GOOG) (NASDAQ:GOOGL) Waymo fleet in cumulative autonomous miles by the end of 2027. Such an event would mark a milestone in Tesla's robotaxi development.

Still, it's not the key metric that really matters, because this is a war likely to be won by a different and even more critical metric. It's such a key number that it will arguably determine Tesla's overall value.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Introducing the total cost of ownership (TCO) per mile

It's important to be clear about this number. Going back to the We, Robot event in 2024, Elon Musk outlined that the operating cost of a Cybercab is "probably going to be $0.20" per mile, with "The price of everything would be about $0.30 to $0.40 per mile," with a Cybercab cost of $30,000.

However, these are Tesla's costs, so any individual buying a Cybercab to operate it as a robotaxi needs to factor in the $299-per-month full self-driving (FSD) subscription fee. Assuming a Cybercab is moderately run for 300,000 miles, it could rack up four years of subscriptions worth $14,352 in FSD costs.

Why the number matters so much

By "everything," Musk presumably means the fully loaded cost per mile, which includes Cybercab cost, energy cost, maintenance, cleaning, remote operations, and any other operational costs, in the TCO per-mile target of $0.30.

This is where the battle over robotaxis will be won, because Tesla is highly likely to face competition from rivals developing low-cost electric vehicles (EVs) equipped with autonomous driving software. While its vision-only approach, leadership in EVs, scaling of Cybercab, and lead in the operational learning that will reduce TCO per mile give it a massive initial edge, it does not mean its robotaxi margins can't be eroded over time.

Image source: Tesla.

To illustrate this, consider the following scenario: a Cybercab costing $30,000, with a useful life of 300,000 miles, compared with a low-cost EV robotaxi costing $20,000, with a useful life of 400,000 miles:

The Cybercab's up-front cost is depreciated such that the hardware cost is $30,000/300,000 = $0.10 per mile, and, with $0.20 in operating costs, the TCO per mile is $0.30.

The low-cost rival equivalent is $20,000/400,000 = $0.05 per mile; add $0.20 in operating costs per mile, and the TCO per mile is $0.25.

title: Not Lucid. Not Ford. The EV Stock Most Likely to Catch Every Refunded Cybertruck Buyer.
detail:
Not Lucid. Not Ford. The EV Stock Most Likely to Catch Every Refunded Cybertruck Buyer.
Reuben Gregg Brewer, The Motley Fool
Sun, November 22, 2026 at 5:27 AM MST 5 min read
TSLA
F
RIVN
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Tesla (NASDAQ:TSLA) is no stranger to controversy, at least partly thanks to its polarizing CEO Elon Musk. However, the company's products themselves can be just as "engaging" as its CEO, highlighted by the Cybertruck. Some people loved its looks; others thought it was ugly. Either way, Cybertruck production is ending. Here's why Rivian (NASDAQ:RIVN) could see a huge boost at just the right time as potential Cybertruck customers look elsewhere for an all-electric truck.

Cybertruck: More demand than production

Elon Musk has stated that Tesla is dropping the Cybertruck so it can focus on producing Cybercabs. This may be true to some degree, but there have long been suspicions that the Cybertruck wasn't selling well. That may have changed after the electric vehicle maker announced plans to shut the production line in around eight months, which led to a flood of new orders.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Image source: Rivian Automotive.

That's not actually surprising, as the announcement likely brought forward demand. The cancellation of the Cybertruck could also have pushed people who like to own "exclusive" things, as well as those who like to flip products with limited supply, to jump in line. Regardless, it looks like there's now going to be more demand than supply. If customers still want an all-electric truck after the Cybertruck is no more, there's one vehicle maker that stands out: Rivian.

The end of the Cybertruck couldn't have come at a better time for Rivian

Rivian started out making all-electric high-end trucks and work trucks. The consumer vehicles it makes are stylish and have won multiple awards. However, the cost limited their appeal. This wasn't a tactical mistake; it was part of the plan. Like Tesla, Rivian started at the high end to maximize revenue per vehicle while it built out its business. The long-term goal was to expand production by bringing out a lower-cost, mass-market vehicle.

That vehicle, the R2, has just started to hit the market. It is already Rivian's best-selling model. Notably, the company's revenues rose 38% year over year in the third quarter of 2026, following the R2 launch, with deliveries up 46%. That success isn't surprising, given the R2 is a new, lower-cost model. The real key to Rivian's success is maintaining demand over the long term. Tesla's cancellation of the Cybertruck just increased the chances of that happening.

"I'm not sure what MAGA means, but if that means sort of blind adherence to a set of policies by the Republican Party, then I certainly don't have that," Musk said.

Key Takeaways

Stocks had their worst week of 2026, and angel investor Jason Calacanis said he'll put any free cash he has into SpaceX, Tesla, Uber, Shopify and Google.

He says big tech trades at its lowest P/Es since the dot-com era. That holds up much better for Alphabet and Uber than for Tesla.

Tesla trades at 162x forward earnings, well above its five-year average, while Uber's 16x is its lowest in three years.

SpaceX looks cheap only against 2027 earnings, so Uber is the strongest bargain on the list.

Stocks just had their worst week of 2026, and SpaceX (SPCX:NASDAQ), Tesla (TSLA:NASDAQ), Uber Technologies (UBER:NYSE) and Alphabet (GOOG) are at the top of one well-known investor's shopping list.

The S&P 500 fell 9% last week, its worst week since April 2025, and the Nasdaq dropped 10%. On this weekend's episode of This Week in Startups, angel investor Jason Calacanis said people are "capitulating totally on big tech companies." He added that those companies now trade at their lowest P/Es since the dot-com era.

His response?

"I am going to catch every knife in the stock market I can. Any amount of free cash I have, I'm buying SpaceX, Tesla, Uber, Shopify, Google…"

(He also admitted, "I haven't bought any yet, but I will.")

A day earlier, he told bitcoin holders on X to sell at least half their position if they're up and move it into the same names, plus Amazon, Apple and Meta.

But those knives are falling from very different heights.

Tesla's multiple is still sky-high

Tesla's forward P/E has come down a long way from its peak, but it's still far above its own average:

Tesla (TSLA): forward (NTM) P/E, last 5 years (TIKR)

At 162x forward earnings, Tesla's multiple is down by a third from its 243x peak last December. That still leaves it well above the 108x it averaged over the past five years. Next year's estimates don't help much either. In an X exchange about a possible Tesla-SpaceX merger, Future Fund's Gary Black put Tesla at 168x 2027 earnings. Whatever Tesla is, it isn't trading anywhere near a dot-com-era low.

At 19x, Alphabet trades below its 22x five-year average and far below the 33x it reached at the end of April. That makes it a stock the selloff really did mark down, even though it's still above the 16x it hit in April 2025. For scale, Tesla's multiple is more than 8x Alphabet's.

title: Tesla Just Started Selling Cybercabs, Here's What It Means for a SpaceX and Tesla Merger .
detail:
Tesla Just Started Selling Cybercabs, Here's What It Means for a SpaceX and Tesla Merger .
Lee Samaha, The Motley Fool
Sun, November 22, 2026 at 12:25 AM MST 4 min read
TSLA
SPCX
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

The news that Tesla(NASDAQ:TSLA)is inviting select customers to buy Cybercabs isn't a game changer from a financial perspective (at least not immediately). Still, it is highly symbolic and highlights the case for Tesla shareholders holding fire on agreeing to a potential merger with Space Exploration Technologies (NASDAQ:SPCX) (or SpaceX for short). Here's why.

Tesla starts selling Cybercabs.

In itself, buying a Cybercab right now is hardly an attractive option for most people. They are reported to cost $29,990, but they can't be used without a $299 monthly subscription, they lack manual driving controls (a steering wheel, pedals, etc.), and they can only operate in the limited geo-fenced areas where the robotaxi service currently operates.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

However, they will obviously attract Tesla enthusiasts, social media influencers, and those confident in widespread regulatory approvals for Tesla's robotaxi service. To be clear, as management is, it's focused on becoming a transportation-as-a-service company with the "vast majority of the Cybercab stuff will be essentially Tesla-owned and Transport-as-a-Service," according to CEO Elon Musk.

Why the sale of Cybercabs matters

The reality is their sale is more about generating promotional buzz around robotaxis as the company prepares for a widespread expansion in 2027. Fortunately, everything points to a quantum leap in the robotaxi rollout next year. The company continues to develop its next major upgrade of its full self-driving software, namely v15, which should be validated and released by early 2027.

Image source: Tesla.

Also, Cybercab production is ramping up, and Tesla says it's gathering data on unsupervised miles with its robotaxi at a double-digit weekly growth rate.

What it means for a SpaceX and Tesla merger

After years of delays and missed timelines, everything points to Tesla finally releasing value from its robotaxi service next year. At which point, its investors are entitled to ask whether it would make sense to agree to a merger with SpaceX before the robotaxi ramps up.

While an offer is not on the table, and investors don't know the terms of a deal, or whether there will even be one, it's hard not to think that a robotaxi ramp-up in 2027 would increase Tesla's share price.

Cathie Wood, Brad Gerstner and 16 Other Big Funds Bought Tesla Last Quarter, While 15 Sold. Who's Right? ©U.S. Air Force photo by Trevor Cokley and Bl∡ke from Pexels via Canva
Key Takeaways

Of the 460 big funds that have filed 13Fs for the quarter ended Sept. 30, 18 bought Tesla and 15 sold, with Brad Gerstner's Altimeter Capital and Cathie Wood's ARK Invest among the buyers.

The buyers made the bigger bets: Altimeter's and Viking Global's purchases were each larger than the three biggest sales combined.

Tesla trades at 162x forward earnings, against a five-year average of 108x and about 6x for General Motors, which Viking sold out of in the same quarter.

Analysts expect 2028 earnings only just above 2023's and negative free cash flow through 2028, so the sellers have the better case on today's numbers.

The 13Fs are in, and big money couldn't agree on Tesla (TSLA:NASDAQ). Filings for the quarter ended Sept. 30, the last of them due Nov. 16, show 18 big funds bought the stock while 15 sold.

The counts cover the 460 big funds that have filed for the quarter. Those are funds readers know or funds holding $1 billion or more of US stocks, with quant and index funds left out. A buyer opened a position or added 20% or more to its shares, and a seller sold out or cut 20% or more. In all, 62 of the 460 held Tesla on Sept. 30.

The buyers went big

Brad Gerstner's Altimeter Capital made the biggest buy. It opened a new position of 1.92 million shares, worth about $680 million at the Sept. 30 price. Tesla ended the quarter at 6.9% of its 13F stocks, its fourth-largest of 16 holdings.

Andreas Halvorsen's Viking Global, which manages $78.2 billion, came next. It more than quadrupled its stake, adding about $636 million of stock to finish at 2.34 million shares, 3% of its 13F stocks. In the same quarter, Viking sold all 5.01 million of its shares of General Motors (GM:NASDAQ), a stake worth $386 million on June 30.

Cathie Wood's ARK Invest added 22%, about $217 million worth. Tesla was its largest holding on Sept. 30: 3.37 million shares worth $1.20 billion, 6.9% of its 13F stocks. H&H International Investment, which manages $25.5 billion, added 21% to reach 4.08 million shares, 8.4% of its 13F stocks.

title: Tesla (TSLA) Stock Looks Richly Priced After Its 47% Three Year Run
detail:
Tesla (TSLA) Stock Looks Richly Priced After Its 47% Three Year Run
Mitch Lawler
Sat, November 21, 2026 at 2:08 PM MST 4 min read
TSLA
Trade Tesla on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Tesla has been busy reshaping its business around robotaxis, humanoid robots and energy projects while the share price has swung sharply, and that leaves a basic question for you as an investor. Is the current US$345.82 price tag adequately backed by what the company is generating through its sales today?

Over the past 3 years the stock has gained 46.9%, which puts a lot of weight on whether recent top line performance can carry that kind of market value.

A planned €3b expansion of the Berlin Gigafactory for Cybercab production, along with large new projects in chips and solar, can reshape future revenue but also means heavier near term spending that matters for how you think about sales based valuation.

Your read on Tesla is one view; the desks covering it have another. See what analysts think Tesla's shares could be worth.

The issue now is whether Tesla's current share price is justified by its sales once you line it up against the Fair Ratio benchmark.

If you are weighing Tesla's US$345.82 share price against its current sales, it can help to see how other companies tied to AI infrastructure are valued through our 53 AI infrastructure stocks.

Does Tesla Look Pricey on Sales?

P/S is a useful lens for Tesla because so much of the story revolves around what each dollar of revenue could one day be worth rather than today's accounting earnings. On this metric, the stock trades on a P/S of 13.2x, compared with an auto industry average of 0.4x and a peer group around 1.1x. Investors are therefore paying a much richer tag for every unit of current sales than is typical in the sector.

The Fair Ratio, which adjusts for Tesla's growth profile, margins, size and risk, indicates that this P/S level screens as overvalued, and the gap is wide enough that the model functions more as a warning signal than a precise target. Despite the fresh wave of capital intensive projects in robotaxis, chips and solar, along with the planned €3b Berlin expansion, the current P/S still reflects very high expectations for what those ventures will eventually deliver in revenue terms.
